https://www.dw.com/en/germany-s-long-roa.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5I5oA The Civil Partnership Act was just one step towards same-sex marriage Image: Sven Hoppe/dpa/picture alliance Advertisement August 1, 2001, marked a turning point: with the Civil Partnership Act, same-sex couples in Germany gained a legal framework for the registration of their partnerships. However, another 16 years would pass before marriage itself became an option. "The Civil Partnership Act was a milestone for the legal recognition of same-sex couples in Germany and laid the foundation for opening up marriage," Alexander Vogt of the national board of " Queere Vielfalt e.V. " (Queer diversity) told DW. "It introduced a legally secure partnership with rights similar to those of marriage — such as inheritance, maintenance, and residency rights — though it remained discriminatory in many areas – like adoption or tax law. Nevertheless, it gave us a foot in the door — a solid base from which further rights could be secured, usually by appealing to the Federal Constitutional Court ." Reinhard Lüschow (r) and Heinz-Friedrich Harre were the first same-sex couple in Germany to register under the new Civil Partnership Act Image: picture alliance/dpa Public opinion was ahead of the political establishment The legislation was preceded by a fierce political debate. The opposition bloc of conservative parties, the Christian Democratic Union and the Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU), denounced it as an "unconstitutional attack on marriage and the family." Lawmakers from the ruling center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), however, described the law as "a long-overdue act of redress." "There was strong conservative opposition, for instance from churches and civic groups," Alexander Vogt noted. "The debate reflected the classic culture war between traditional and progressive values." Backed by the governing coalition of Social Democrats and Greens , the majority of Bundestag lawmakers voted in favor of the Civil Partnership Act in November 2000, despite opposition from the CDU/CSU and the neoliberal Free Democrats (FDP). German public opinion was already a step ahead: A 1999 survey showed that 55% of respondents were already in favor of the Civil Partnership Act. However, Germany was by no means a pioneer. Denmark was the first country in the world to introduce civil partnerships for same-sex couples, doing so as early as 1989. Norway, Sweden, and Iceland followed in the mid-1990s, with France following in 1999. Two fathers, two babies To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video 'We simply wanted equal treatment' Twenty-five years ago, Reinhard Lüschow and his husband Heinz-Friedrich Harre — who has since passed away — became the first same-sex couple in Germany to tie the knot at a registry office under the new Civil Partnership Act. They had spent the preceding decade fighting for legal recognition as a couple. As early as 1992, they had made a public statement by applying to register their marriage — in a coordinated move by 250 male and female same-sex couples across Germany. When their application was rejected, they took the case all the way to the Federal Constitutional Court. "We simply wanted to be treated equally," Lüschow recently told the Protestant Press Service (epd). Although the court ruled at the time that marriage was a union between a man and a woman, it also mandated that the legislature ensure same-sex partnerships were not discriminated against. When the Bundestag implemented this requirement through the Civil Partnership Act, Lüschow and Harre reacted immediately. Hard-won changes The Civil Partnership Act regulates matters such as the use of surnames, mutual financial support, and inheritance rights. In the years that followed, the scope of civil partnerships was gradually expanded — first in 2004 to include stepchild adoption, and later to achieve tax equality following several rulings by the Federal Constitutional Court. What do weddings look like in Germany? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The Civil Partnership Act was merely the first step toward equality. The decisive step did not come until October 1, 2017, with legislation that introduced so-called "marriage for all." This, too, was a hard-won victory. The conservative parties had come to power again in 2005. They blocked the legislation until Chancellor Angela Merkel authorized a vote free from party-line constraints, meaning lawmakers were to follow only their consciences; this is how the majority was secured in 2017. Angela Merkel and current Chancellor Friedrich Merz voted against the legislation. Bodo Mende and Karl Kreile were the first same-sex couple to marry. Reflecting on the 2001 Civil Partnership Act, Mende later told DW: "It was a second-class partnership." Although there were few legal restrictions, the status lacked the standing of a conventional marriage. Married partners enjoy more rights — for instance, regarding naming laws, child adoption, and the equalization of pension rights. Marriage also carries greater recognition internationally. According to the Federal Statistical Office, around 108,000 couples had availed themselves of this new option by 2025. At the same time, approximately 24,000 registered civil partnerships remain in existence; these can be converted into marriages upon application. Bodo Mende and Karl Kreile (r) were the first same-sex couple to marry in Germany in 2017 Image: Britta Pedersen/dpa-Zentralbild/ZB/picture alliance 'Marriage for all' does not amount to full equality Differences remain between same-sex and opposite-sex couples. Alexander Vogt of the association Queere Vielfalt cites an example regarding the law of parentage: "If a child is born into a family with two mothers, the non-biological mother must first go through an adoption process to establish legal parenthood. This is not the case for heterosexual couples." Reflecting on societal developments, Vogt observes: "Acceptance of same-sex marriage has clearly increased." However, he adds: "We have become more visible in recent years, but not safer; violence and hate crimes — particularly against queer people — have risen sharply. The figures have increased tenfold since 2010! The attack in Berlin represents a tragic peak in this trend, one that has garnered significant public attention." https://www.bursa.ro/the-campaign-agains.text: President Nicuşor Dan has nominated Liberal MEP Siegfried Mureşan as the candidate for Prime Minister, following more than four months of political crisis and two failed attempts to form a government. According to the head of state, Mureşan was the person who garnered the most support during consultations with the parties, even though a parliamentary majority has not yet taken shape. Furthermore, it is worth noting that the "BURSA" newspaper had already highlighted-in its edition from Friday, September 18-the President's unusually blunt warning: the negotiations revealed "more electoral posturing" than concern for the country's stability. 28813066 The nomination should have put to rest at least one of the accusations leveled against Nicuşor Dan: that he was stalling the appointment of a Prime Minister and that the resulting deadlock could justify his suspension. It did not. It merely changed the nature of the attack. Petrişor Peiu, the leader of the AUR senators, immediately predicted that Mureşan would either resign his mandate before the vote or achieve a "ridiculous" result in Parliament. Gheorghe Piperea announced that AUR would not vote for the future cabinet. The party did not even wait for the governing program, the list of ministers, or the conclusion of negotiations; the verdict had been decided before the case was even heard. The reactions of AUR leaders indicate that the nomination is not viewed as a potential way out of the crisis, but rather as a stage that could lead to a failed investiture vote and, potentially, early elections. 06913065 This reveals the political trap in which AUR is attempting to ensnare the President. If Nicuşor Dan fails to nominate a candidate, the delay becomes proof of his alleged disregard for the Constitution. If he nominates a candidate who does not belong to AUR and refuses to accept the party's conditions, AUR will withhold its support, contribute to the failure of the investiture, and frame the resulting crisis as yet another failure on the part of the President. Indeed, AUR leader George Simion stated after the consultations at Cotroceni that AUR would only vote for a government in which it participates. In a third scenario-were the head of state to accept a prime minister imposed or politically controlled by AUR-the party would gain access to executive power and governmental resources while simultaneously pursuing the parliamentary process to suspend the President. Although the government plays no formal constitutional role in the suspension procedure-a matter resting with Parliament and, ultimately, the voters-controlling the Executive would grant AUR an incomparably stronger political and institutional position. In all three scenarios, AUR stands to gain something: grounds for impeachment, the prospect of early elections, or a share of executive power. The only option the party seems unwilling to accept is political stabilization achieved without its involvement. *The campaign that didn't end in May 2025 This behavior did not begin with the nomination of Siegfried Mureşan; rather, it should be viewed as an extension of the presidential campaign George Simion lost in May 2025. Since then, AUR has acted more like a party in a perpetual state of campaigning than a political group that adjusts its tactics for the periods between elections. The themes may shift-government formation, the justice system, policy regarding Ukraine, alleged constitutional violations, Romania's representation abroad-but they all fit into the same narrative: that Nicuşor Dan lacks political legitimacy as president and should be removed from office. In this type of campaign, impeachment is no longer the exceptional remedy prescribed by the Constitution for serious misconduct. Instead, it becomes a campaign brand, a tool for mobilization, and a means of keeping society in the charged atmosphere of a presidential runoff election. Tangible evidence of this is the "suspend.ro" platform itself, used to pressure lawmakers and rally public support. An investigation by Public Record revealed that the domain was registered using details linked to Nicolae Capcelea, the owner of Follow Digital Solutions. During the 2024 and 2025 campaigns, the firm received over 10.6 million lei from AUR for online electioneering. This amount cannot be automatically attributed to the suspension platform, but the link between the digital infrastructure of AUR's election campaigns and the new campaign against the president is documented. Consequently, we are not dealing merely with isolated political statements. We see a repeated objective, a dedicated platform, communication resources, and a strategy whereby every crisis is transformed into a new episode of the electoral campaign. *A candidate challenged before even being heard Siegfried Mureşan is neither a flashy candidate nor one built for confrontation. This is, in all likelihood, precisely his problem within the current political equation. He is an economist, a Member of the European Parliament since 2014, and a vice-chair of both the European People's Party and the EPP Group in the European Parliament. He has participated in negotiations regarding EU budgets and major economic dossiers, following studies in Bucharest and Berlin and professional experience in the Bundestag. In other words, he is a logical choice for a country in need of European negotiations, financial stability, and the restoration of its international credibility. One need not share his political views to acknowledge that he possesses a civilized, predictable, and competent profile. Such characterizations are, of course, a matter of judgment; the experience underpinning them, however, is verifiable. Mureşan may face criticism regarding the program he proposes, the ministers he selects, or any concessions made to political parties. Yet none of these factors existed at the moment AUR was already declaring his bid a failure. The candidate was challenged before he had even presented a government lineup. This haste speaks volumes about the detractors' agenda rather than the candidate himself. If the priority were the formation of a functional executive, the parties would be negotiating the program and the cabinet's composition. If the goal is to prolong the crisis until impeachment proceedings or snap elections, the identity of the prime minister becomes almost secondary. *Who benefits from the crisis The crisis directly benefits AUR. The party is leading in the polls and could gain more power through snap elections. According to an analysis published by Reuters, an early vote would benefit George Simion's party, whereas prolonged instability puts pressure on the country's credit rating, investments, and Romania's ability to implement economic measures. Thus, the party's benefit and the country's interest do not align. Romania needs a government, budgetary predictability, and access to European funds. AUR needs the current majority to fail, the president to appear powerless, and society to remain mobilized against a constant adversary. This observation does not prove the existence of an external command structure, nor is it sufficient to claim that all of AUR's actions are coordinated by a foreign power. Russia is the obvious geopolitical beneficiary of the weakening of a state on NATO's eastern flank, the undermining of pro-European institutions, and the ongoing conflict regarding support for Ukraine. However, strategic benefit alone does not constitute proof of a command relationship. Such an accusation would require documents, financial trails, or operational evidence that have not been made public. What "can" be demonstrated is the internal mechanism: AUR maintains a state of perpetual campaigning, turns institutional deadlock into political capital, and keeps the suspension of Nicuşor Dan as an objective, regardless of the president's actual decision. The nomination of Siegfried Mureşan makes this mechanism easier to observe. The president nominated a candidate with experience and the broadest support available from the consultations. AUR did not respond by negotiating a solution, but by declaring its failure. Therefore, the essential question is no longer what reason AUR will cite for the suspension. The grounds cited can be found or changed from one week to the next. The question is whether the suspension represents the conclusion of a constitutional assessment or if it has become the starting point of the entire strategy. The facts to date point to the latter: the political objective was established first, and the justifications were sought afterwards.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqkg.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, The South African former ICC judge was awarded the prize on Friday By George Wright Published 1 hour ago Navi Pillay, the winner of this year's Nobel Peace Prize, has called US sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) "unheard of" and "unacceptable". The South African former ICC judge was awarded the prize on Friday "for her efforts to promote peace and international law", which paved the way for a "more comprehensive global legal order", the Nobel committee said. US President Donald Trump expressed his disatisfaction with the pick and hours later the US unveiled sweeping sanctions in a significant acceleration of its attempt to "dismantle" what it described as a "rogue" institution. The ICC said the measures were an assault on the rule of law and the foundations of the international legal order. Pillay, speaking via video link during an event at the Nobel Peace Center in Oslo on Saturday, said: "There is so much tension and anxiety over the continued existence of international courts, mainly the International Criminal Court in The Hague. "Most importantly, sanctions have been announced by one country against the judges, just for the judicial orders they issue. This is unheard of, unacceptable." US Secretary of State Marco Rubio earlier said the sanctions - which include a ban on US entities making transactions with the ICC - were intended to "defend US sovereignty" and accused the court of seeking to prosecute Americans. The US has already sanctioned 17 ICC judges and officials, but this move sanctions the court itself as an institution and is intended to inhibit its ability to operate financially. However, the US has provided a six-month grace period before some of these latest sanctions kick in, meaning member states can keep paying for its operations - a move Washington says is to allow countries time to negotiate a "solution to address" US concerns. The Trump administration claims that the ICC is run by what it calls globalists who threaten American sovereignty. It is furious over a past investigation into actions of US soldiers in Afghanistan the court has since closed and by its arrest warrants for Israeli officials including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The new sanctions, however, do not say that those warrants must be withdrawn before the measures can be lifted. UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres called the US decision "a serious blow to our collective pursuit of international criminal justice, of which the ICC is a key pillar". The UK joined Canada, Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, Japan and the Netherlands in saying they "regret and strongly disagree with" the sanctions. Figure caption, Watch: Who is Nobel Peace Prize winner Navi Pillay? Pillay, 85, also served as UN rights chief, taking part in high-profile work considering allegations of human rights violations, including in Rwanda, Myanmar and Gaza. Her early work included defending anti-apartheid activists in South Africa, and on Friday she became the country's fifth Peace Prize winner - following in the footsteps of Nelson Mandela and Archbishop Desmond Tutu. "If you clap a little bit more I may share this prize with Trump," she joked after receiving the prize, a reference to last year's winner, Venezuelan opposition figure MarÃ­a Corina Machado, deciding to gift her prize to the US president. Trump called the announcement of Pillay as 2026's winner "disgraceful and embarassing", and an "indelible stain on the country of Norway". He has long indicated he thought he should have been awarded the prestigious prize, and was nominated by several allies for it last year. https://www.dw.com/en/west-bank-us-journ.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5OLUj Veteran photojournalist Heidi Levine said she was attacked and pushed to the ground Image: Debbie Hill/UPI Photo/Newscom/picture alliance Advertisement Washington Post journalist Heidi Levine was injured on Friday after being attacked by a group of Israeli settlers while on assignment in the occupied West Bank , according to the publication. The Post said that the incident took place near the village of Abu Falah, northeast of Ramallah, and involved "dozens of masked Israeli settlers" who attacked Palestinian villagers gathering the autumn olive harvest. Washington Post says Levine clearly identifiable Matt Murray, the paper's executive editor, called for an investigation into the incident. "This morning, a Washington Post photographer, Heidi Levine, was attacked by Israeli settlers while reporting in the West Bank,” Murray said. Levine is a US citizen. "She was wearing visible markings clearly identifying her as a journalist. While we are relieved that Heidi has received medical care and is safe, we are outraged by this unwarranted attack on a journalist doing her job and urge a thorough investigation and follow-through from authorities." Speaking from a hospital bed later, veteran photojournalist Levine, who is in stable condition, said: "I was attacked, pushed to the ground. Luckily I had my flak jacket and helmet, otherwise I probably wouldn't even be here, because they just kept kicking me and kicking me." Blogger Andrey Khrzhanovskiy filmed the incident and told The Post that the settlers beat Levine with sticks while journalists and villagers were forced back. Palestinian American watches as West Bank house under siege To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Netanyahu's office says facts 'remain unclear' The office of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu issued a statement saying it was not yet clear exactly what had happened. "The facts surrounding the confrontation near Abu Falah, during which Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine was allegedly assaulted, remain unclear and are under investigation. Netanyahu's office went on to say there were reports that "some 200 Arabs and far-left activists confronted approximately 40 Israeli youths." It said that there was footage of masked individuals from both sides "hurling objects." "Other footage appears to show Levine knocked down and immediately helped to her feet by the same unidentified individual. The investigation must establish the facts, including who initiated the violence," Netanyahu's office said. The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said that both the IDF and the Israel Border Police attended the scene. "Foreign media personnel were present at the scene and a female journalist was injured during the confrontation. All details of the incident will be examined. Upon arriving to the scene, the forces acted to disperse the confrontation using riot dispersal means," the IDF said in a statement on X. "The IDF strongly condemns this incident. Attempts to incite friction between populations undermine security in the area," the IDF said. US condemns 'criminal violence' The US said it condemned "criminal violence by any party" in the occupied West Bank. "We condemn criminal violence by any party in the West Bank and support appropriate investigations as well as legal accountability for those responsible," the AFP news agency quoted a State Department official as saying, on condition of anonymity, without directly criticizing the settlers. "The Department has reached out to the Washington Post to offer consular assistance," the official told AFP. US Democratic Senator Chris Coons of Connecticut, in a post on X, called the attack "appalling" and said "there must be swift justice and accountability for perpetrators of violent extremism in the West Bank, which stands in the way of regional peace and is escalating an already unpredictable and dangerous situation." EU to impose new sanctions against Israeli settlers To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Attack condemned by press association and advocacy group The Foreign Press Association represents international media in Israel and the Palestinian territories and said Levine's passport, phone, wallet and equipment were stolen by the attackers. "This is the latest in a long line of violent attacks by Israeli settlers against journalists and other civilians in the occupied West Bank," it said. "Yet our repeated calls for action to confront this lawlessness have been ignored by Israeli authorities," it added. International press watchdog Reporters Without Borders strongly condemned the attack and called on Israeli authorities to "put an end to this impunity and prosecute the perpetrators of this heinous assault." "This brazen violence... is evidence of the impunity with which extremist Jewish settlers operate, often under the protection of Israeli armed forces," added the advocacy group, known by its French initials RSF. https://www.kiro7.com/news/local/diners-.text: Local ‘Diners, Drive-Ins and Dives’ favorite closing in Lakewood after 16 years By MyNorthwest.com Staff October 14, 2026 at 8:21 am PDT Enter Fullscreen Expand Diners sit inside Bruno's European Restaurant in Lakewood. (Bruno's European Restaurant) By MyNorthwest.com Staff October 14, 2026 at 8:21 am PDT LAKEWOOD, Wash. — Bruno’s European Restaurant in Lakewood is closing up shop this Saturday after 16 years. The restaurant, which served schnitzel, pierogies, and traditional German-Polish favorites, appeared on Guy Fieri’s “Diners, Drive-Ins and Dives” in 2013. “When you’re on the hunt for hearty, home-style European food in Washington, Bruno’s European Restaurant in Tacoma is a must-stop on your foodie road trip map,” “Diners, Drive-Ins and Dives” stated on its website . “This family-run gem may be young in years, but it’s already become a beloved local staple, serving up soul-warming Polish and German classics in a charming, authentically European setting. Think traditional German waitress attire, warm hospitality, and a kitchen that feels like it’s cooking straight from grandma’s recipe book.” Bruno’s owners, Krystyna and Bruno Tomaszewska, told The Tacoma News Tribune they couldn’t commit to a new five-year lease and needed to focus on their health. Krystyna is in her late 70s, while Bruno is in his late 60s. They’re preparing to retire after decades in the restaurant business. News of Bruno’s closure has circulated since they told their staff, about 10 employees, during their Oktoberfest celebration on Sept. 26. People within Lakewood and surrounding areas have been clamoring to get the eatery’s most famous entrees, including its “hangover soup” — a hearty bowl of soup with Eastern European and Polish roots filled with rich broth, chunks of meat, sausage, bacon, pork loin, diced potatoes, mushrooms, carrots, celery, leeks, onions, garlic, crushed tomatoes, dill pickles, and sour cream. Their hangover soup was called the standout on the menu by “Diners, Drive-Ins and Dives,” followed by the beef roulade, the three schnitzel plate, and the death by chocolate cake. Their daughter-in-law will continue in the industry as Krystyna and Bruno enter retirement, having her own Bavarian-themed, home-cooked-style restaurant in Black Diamond. ©2026 Cox Media Group 0 View Comments Most Read
